# Licensing

Rimsky ships under two licenses, split at one line. The wire contract you implement or link against to speak to rimsky is Apache License 2.0. Everything else rimsky ships — the orchestrator, the CLI, the bundled services, every image — is GNU AGPL v3.0-or-later, with a Fall Guy Consulting commercial license as the alternative. Rimsky is Copyright © 2026 Fall Guy Consulting.

| You are… | Your obligation |
| --- | --- |
| Implementing or linking against the protocols module | Apache 2.0. Permissive, no copyleft. |
| Running, modifying, or offering the rest of rimsky under open terms | AGPL-3.0-or-later. Copyleft, including network-service source disclosure. |
| Doing the above but unable to accept the AGPL | Buy a commercial license: licensing@fallguyconsulting.com. |

Running a rimsky image over a network puts you in the second row. The escape hatch from that row is not a smaller image — it is implementing the protocols from your own process, which the first row covers.

## The bright line

The Apache surface is the `lib/protocols` module: the ten `.proto` wire definitions, the generated bindings, and the helper and conformance packages a consumer implements or links against. Rimsky keeps it permissive so anyone can build a service that talks to rimsky without taking on copyleft.

The AGPL surface is everything else rimsky ships: the foundation, graph, runtime, and control layers; the bundled services; the binaries; the test and tools trees. These are runnable artifacts, not illustrations. Using one is using rimsky.

The line holds mechanically. The protocols module imports nothing internal, so the Apache code is a single closed island and no Apache file can depend on an AGPL file. At this release the repository carries 92 Apache-licensed source files and 1,623 AGPL-licensed source files.

## What each license asks of you

**Apache 2.0.** Use, modify, and redistribute, including inside closed-source products. Preserve the license and copyright notices and the `NOTICE` file.

**AGPL-3.0-or-later.** Strong copyleft. If you modify rimsky and convey it, or make it available to users over a network, you must offer those users the corresponding source under the AGPL. The network clause is §13, and it is what separates the AGPL from the GPL. No action is required to use rimsky under these terms — the AGPL is the default.

**Fall Guy Consulting commercial license.** A separately negotiated grant over the same AGPL-licensed code, for organizations that want to use, modify, or distribute the orchestrator and services without the §5 copyleft or §13 network-disclosure obligations. It does not change the Apache terms on the protocols module. Contact licensing@fallguyconsulting.com.

## Published packages

Eleven artifacts are published at a release.

| Package | License |
| --- | --- |
| `github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core` (Go module) | AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial |
| `github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/lib/protocols` (Go module) | Apache-2.0 |
| `@rimsky-ai/protocols` (npm) | Apache-2.0 |
| `protoDir` and `protoPath` (npm package exports) | Apache-2.0 |
| `rimsky_<version>_linux_amd64.tar.gz` (GitHub release archive) | AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial |
| `rimsky_<version>_linux_arm64.tar.gz` (GitHub release archive) | AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial |
| `rimsky_<version>_darwin_amd64.tar.gz` (GitHub release archive) | AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial |
| `rimsky_<version>_darwin_arm64.tar.gz` (GitHub release archive) | AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial |
| `checksums.txt` (GitHub release) | Checksums over the archives; carries no license of its own |

Importing the root Go module puts AGPL code in your build. The module holds the CLI, the role binaries, and the graph, runtime, and control layers, and nothing in it is Apache. Import the `lib/protocols` module instead when you want the permissive surface alone; it is tagged separately, as `lib/protocols/vX.Y.Z`.

The npm package ships the ten `.proto` files and the two exports `protoDir` and `protoPath`. Both code files carry an `SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0` header, and `package.json` declares `"license": "Apache-2.0"`.

Each release archive carries the `rimsky` CLI binary together with `LICENSE.agpl`, `LICENSE.apache`, `NOTICE`, `COPYRIGHT`, and `COPYING.md`. A release also generates an SBOM for every archive.

## Images

Fifteen images are published to `docker.io/rimskyai`. Every one of them carries AGPL-3.0-or-later-or-commercial rimsky code, because every one of them is a rimsky binary.

Core images: `rimsky`, `rimsky-all-in-one`, `rimsky-host-daemon-proxy`, `rimsky-conformance`.

Bundled-service images: `rimsky-claim-producer-filesystem`, `rimsky-claim-producer-postgres`, `rimsky-sensor-cron`, `rimsky-sensor-http`, `rimsky-sensor-object-store`, `rimsky-sensor-webhook`, `rimsky-subscriber-openlineage`, `rimsky-executor-http-node`, `rimsky-executor-verifier-http`, `rimsky-executor-verifier-shape-checks`, `rimsky-executor-claude-agent`.

The bundled services are AGPL like the orchestrator. They are real services rimsky offers you ready to run, so running one is running rimsky. If you want a producer, sensor, executor, or subscriber outside the AGPL, write it against the Apache protocols and run it in your own process.

Fourteen of the fifteen images build on Google's distroless static base and add nothing but rimsky's own statically linked binaries and configuration files. The base image carries its own upstream licenses, which rimsky neither restates nor alters.

`rimsky-executor-claude-agent` is the exception, and the one image whose contents you must review beyond rimsky's own terms. Its runtime layer is a Chainguard Wolfi base with `git` and `tini` installed, plus a pinned build of Anthropic's Claude Code CLI, which the executor spawns as a subprocess. That CLI is third-party software distributed under Anthropic's own terms, not under rimsky's. Read those terms before you redistribute this image.

## Third-party dependencies

Rimsky vendors no third-party source into the repository. Dependencies arrive at build time through Go modules, and the `NOTICE` file records that no third-party Apache-licensed source is bundled today.

The repository enumerates third-party licenses for the Apache surface only. It names each module the permissive surface may depend on and restricts them to Apache-2.0, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC, and MIT. The license check rejects any module in the Apache module's build closure that is unlisted or carries a license outside that set, so contamination of the permissive surface fails the build rather than shipping.

The AGPL surface's dependency licenses are not enumerated in the repository. Get that inventory from the SBOM instead. Every published image carries an SBOM attestation listing every OS package and Go module in each layer, alongside a provenance attestation recording the source repository, builder, and build arguments.

## How to tell which license a file carries

Read the per-file header. Apache files carry:

```
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
```

AGPL files carry:

```
SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-or-later OR LicenseRef-FallGuy-Commercial
```

`LicenseRef-FallGuy-Commercial` is a non-registry SPDX pointer to the commercial alternative. It is not a public license text.

The authoritative path map is `licensing.yml`, which classifies by longest-prefix match, so a specific subdirectory can override its parent's bucket. The map covers `.go`, `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.proto`, `.sql`, and `.sh` files. The `license-check` tool verifies that every such file carries the right header, that no Apache file imports an AGPL package, that every path the map names still exists, and that the Apache build closure stays permissive. If a header and the map ever disagree, that is a bug the tool catches.

## Where the artifacts fall short of what you would expect

**No published image declares its license.** Images carry no `org.opencontainers.image.licenses` label, so tooling that reads that label finds nothing and infers nothing. Three images set a title and description label; none sets a license label. No image bundles a license text file either — the distroless and Wolfi runtime layers hold only the rimsky binary and its runtime dependencies. Treat `COPYING.md`, `COPYRIGHT`, and the per-file headers in the repository as the license signal for every image, and carry those texts yourself if you redistribute an image.

**Docker Hub's "No AGPL v3 licenses" green check does not mean the image is AGPL-free.** That check scans the third-party supply chain — OS packages, Go modules, npm packages — for AGPL-licensed code pulled in as a dependency. Rimsky's own binaries are AGPL and are built from this repository rather than pulled as a dependency, so they do not appear in that scan. Whoever runs these images runs AGPL software, whatever the badge shows.

**The npm package and the protocols Go module ship no license text.** The npm tarball contains thirteen entries: the ten `.proto` files, `index.js`, `index.d.ts`, and `package.json`. It carries no `LICENSE` file and no `NOTICE`. The protocols Go module's zip is likewise limited to its own directory tree, which holds no license text. The Apache grant reaches you through the SPDX header on every shipped file and the `license` field in `package.json`. Take the Apache text and the `NOTICE` file from the repository or from a release archive when you need to satisfy the Apache attribution requirement.

**The repository has no plain `LICENSE` file.** The full texts live in `LICENSE.apache` and `LICENSE.agpl`. Tooling that looks for a file named `LICENSE` at the repository root reports none.

**The license check reports violations at this release.** It flags 116 unclassified source files, all of them under the project's own planning records rather than under any shipped surface. No published package and no image contains them. The Apache and AGPL buckets themselves report zero violations: no missing or wrong header, no Apache-to-AGPL import, no missing path, no impermissibly licensed dependency in the Apache closure.

## Contributions

Contributions are accepted under the Rimsky Contributor Certificate in `CONTRIBUTING.md`. Every non-merge commit in a pull request must carry a `Rimsky-Cert:` trailer, which certifies the standard provenance claims and grants Fall Guy Consulting the rights needed to maintain the multi-license structure, including the commercial track. A GitHub Action checks every commit for a well-formed trailer and reports a required check, so a pull request whose commits are not all signed off cannot be merged.

## Trademarks

"Rimsky" and the rimsky logo are trademarks of Fall Guy Consulting. A software license is not a trademark license. The usage policy is `TRADEMARKS.md`.

## The binding files

This document is a guide. Where it and these files differ, these files control.

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `LICENSE.apache` | Full Apache License 2.0 text. |
| `LICENSE.agpl` | Full GNU AGPL v3 text. |
| `COPYRIGHT` | The formal per-layer copyright notice the file headers reference. |
| `NOTICE` | The Apache §4(d) attribution notice. |
| `COPYING.md` | The plain-language compliance guide. |
| `licensing.yml` | The machine-readable boundary map the license check enforces. |
| `CONTRIBUTING.md` | The contributor guide and the Rimsky Contributor Certificate. |
| `TRADEMARKS.md` | The trademark usage policy. |
